In [[algebraic geometry]], a '''torus action''' on an [[algebraic variety]] is a [[group-scheme action|group action]] of an [[algebraic torus]] on the variety. A variety equipped with an action of a torus ''T'' is called a '''<nowiki />''T''-variety'''. In [[differential geometry]], one considers an action of a real or complex torus on a [[manifold]] (or an [[orbifold]]).

A [[normal scheme|normal]] algebraic variety with a torus acting on it in such a way that there is a dense orbit is called a [[toric variety]] (for example, orbit closures that are normal are toric varieties).

== Linear action of a torus ==
A [[group-scheme action|linear action]] of a torus can be simultaneously diagonalized, after extending the base field if necessary: if a torus ''T'' is acting on a finite-dimensional vector space ''V'', then there is a direct sum decomposition:
:<math>V = \bigoplus_{\chi} V_{\chi}</math>
where
*<math>\chi: T \to \mathbb{G}_m</math> is a group homomorphism, a [[Character (mathematics)|character]] of ''T''.
*<math>V_{\chi} = \{ v \in V | t \cdot v = \chi(t) v \}</math>, ''T''-invariant subspace called the weight subspace of weight <math>\chi</math>.

The decomposition exists because the linear action determines (and is determined by) a linear representation <math>\pi: T \to \operatorname{GL}(V)</math> and then <math>\pi(T)</math> consists of commuting [[diagonalizable matrix|diagonalizable linear transformations]], upon extending the base field.

If ''V'' does not have finite dimension, the existence of such a decomposition is tricky but one easy case when decomposition is possible is when ''V'' is a union of finite-dimensional representations (<math>\pi</math> is called [[rational representation|rational]]; see below for an example). Alternatively, one uses [[functional analysis]]; for example, uses a [[Hilbert-space direct sum]].

'''Example''': Let <math>S = k[x_0, \dots, x_n]</math> be a polynomial ring over an infinite field ''k''. Let <math>T = \mathbb{G}_m^r</math> act on it as [[algebra automorphism]]s by: for <math>t = (t_1, \dots, t_r) \in
T</math>
:<math>t \cdot x_i = \chi_i(t) x_i</math>
where
:<math>\chi_i(t) = t_1^{\alpha_{i, 1}} \dots t_r^{\alpha_{i, r}},</math> <math>\alpha_{i, j}</math> = integers.
Then each <math>x_i</math> is a ''T''-weight vector and so a monomial <math>x_0^{m_0} \dots x_r^{m_r}</math> is a ''T''-weight vector of weight <math>
\sum m_i \chi_i</math>. Hence,
:<math>S = \bigoplus_{m_0, \dots m_n \ge 0} S_{m_0 \chi_0 + \dots + m_n \chi_n}.</math>
Note if <math>\chi_i(t) = t</math> for all ''i'', then this is the usual decomposition of the polynomial ring into homogeneous components.

== Białynicki-Birula decomposition ==
The Białynicki-Birula decomposition says that a smooth projective algebraic ''T''-variety admits a ''T''-stable [[cellular decomposition]].

It is often described as algebraic [[Morse theory]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://blog.konradvoelkel.de/2013/04/bialynicki-birula-decomposition/|title=Konrad Voelkel » Białynicki-Birula and Motivic Decompositions «}}</ref>
